title: Cotoletta alla milanese
subtitle: Milanese breaded pork chop on the bone
excerpt: Cotoletta alla milanese is a bone-in chop, breaded and fried in butter until golden. The original uses veal; this version uses a thick pork chop, which gives the same satisfying crunch and keeps well in domestic kitchens. The breadcrumb coat should be fine and even; the butter must be properly hot before the chop goes in.
sourceNotes: Milanese regional recipe. Cotoletta alla milanese is one of the oldest documented Italian meat preparations, described in print in the early 19th century. The pork version is a practical home-cook adaptation. Method drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992), and traditional Lombard sources.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian word for a breaded and fried cutlet; the Milanese version is made with a bone-in chop, while the cutlet is beaten flat and the bone acts as a handle.

content.text: alla milanese is a large, bone-in chop pounded flat and breaded in egg and fine breadcrumbs, then fried in butter until golden on both sides. The bone is left on so the diner can hold it. The crumb should be fine and even; the butter must be foaming before the chop goes in, not just warm.

items.prepNote: bone-in, about 2 cm thick, beaten flat between baking paper to 1 cm

content.text: Place {{pork-chop}} of pork chops between baking paper and beat flat to 1 cm. Set up three dishes: seasoned {{plain-flour}} of flour, beaten {{eggs}} of eggs, and {{breadcrumbs-dried}} of fine breadcrumbs.
Dust each chop in flour, shaking off the excess. Dip in egg, letting the excess drip off. Press firmly into breadcrumbs on both sides. Pat lightly to set the crumb.

Heat {{unsalted-butter}} of butter with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. When the butter is foaming, add the chops. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden. Work in batches so the pan is not crowded. Season with salt immediately. Serve with lemon wedges.

items.cause: Insufficient pressing during breading, or the chop was wet.
items.fix: Pat the chops dry before breading. Press the crumb on firmly from both sides. Rest 5 minutes on a rack before frying.

items.cause: Butter not hot enough when the chop went in.
items.fix: The butter should be foaming but not browning. If it foams and subsides without colour, it is too cool; increase the heat.
Beat to a uniform 1 cm. At that thickness, 3 to 4 minutes per side in a properly hot pan cooks it through.

content.text: Milan's breaded cutlet has been claimed as the inspiration for Wiener Schnitzel; there is historical dispute about which came first. What is clear is that the cotoletta alla milanese has been eaten in Lombardy for at least two centuries, always with lemon on the side, always with the bone. A simple green salad alongside is the traditional accompaniment.
